# Dependency Failure, Installed State and Recovery

This optional Unit 9 extension follows the installed-package investigation.
Use actual dpkg operations to distinguish an unpacked application, a satisfied
dependency, a configured package and a working program. It has its own attempt
and evidence record, separate from the manual-release comparison.

## Scope, equipment and prerequisites

Use an ordinary account in an owned disposable Debian/Ubuntu Linux lab with
Python 3, Bash, `dpkg`, `dpkg-deb` and `dpkg-query`. The driver constructs three
tiny local packages from the supplied source: base 1.0, base 2.0 and app 1.0.
The app declares `Depends: linux-layout-base (>= 2.0)`. No repository download,
maintainer script, trigger, root-owned payload or privileged operation is part
of these packages. The host's installed package database is not the experiment.

The installation root and its database live below one newly created owned
lab. Every dpkg change supplies that root explicitly and records its command
and status. `--force-not-root` permits this ordinary-account demonstration;
it does not waive dependency checks. Never drop the root option, copy these
operations onto the host database, add sudo, or add `--force-depends`. Use the
supplied driver to keep the operation scoped. If the environment cannot run
this lab, retain the diagnostic and resolve its prerequisite rather than
pretending that an installation occurred.

Both roles provide working equipment. Complete the named observation tasks in
`dependency-notes.md`; reference reasoning is not this machine's evidence.
After confirming the IDE import, open those notes first, save/download the
ZIP, extract the role and use its Linux terminal. Browser saves do not execute
dpkg operations. Return observations to the same saved attempt.

## Package dependencies and state

Package metadata describes a version requirement. Here app 1.0 requires base
2.0 or later. Installing an archive can unpack its files before configuration
fails. File presence and even a successful direct program run therefore do not
by themselves establish `install ok installed` state. Read the actual database
state separately. dpkg installs supplied archives and checks relationships;
it does not fetch a missing dependency. APT can plan a repository transaction
and resolve related changes, using its configured metadata and policy.

## 1. Predict and construct the local packages

Predict the first app install's status, whether its file will exist afterward,
its database state, and what will be needed for recovery. Then run:

```bash
uname -s
id -u
dpkg --version
python3 --version
lab_parent=$(mktemp -d)
lab="$lab_parent/dependencies"
bash task.sh init --lab "$lab"
bash task.sh build --lab "$lab"
dpkg-deb --field "$lab/packages/linux-layout-app-1.0.deb" Package Version Depends
dpkg-deb --contents "$lab/packages/linux-layout-app-1.0.deb"
```

Keep the shell open and save the exact `OWNED_LAB` path. The package build
retains this lab account's file ownership and writes a manifest of archive
hashes. It refuses an existing workspace/build; each changed experiment uses
a new lab. Package structure and installed state are different observations.

## 2. Observe the missing dependency without hiding failure

```bash
bash task.sh install-app --lab "$lab"
printf 'INSTALL_STATUS=%s\n' "$?"
bash task.sh query --lab "$lab"
bash task.sh audit --lab "$lab"
bash task.sh run --lab "$lab"
printf 'RUNTIME_STATUS=%s\n' "$?"
```

Expect a nonzero install status and an app that is unpacked but not configured.
`query` asks the separate database for both packages; its own status can be
nonzero while the base is absent. It can also succeed when the dependency name
has a recorded `not-installed` entry. Query success means an entry was found,
not that its package is installed. Read the status field and confirm that the
base payload is absent. Retain stdout, stderr and status separately.
`audit` identifies the incomplete package. The unpacked program should report
a missing dependency file and exit 1. This failure is an intended observation,
not a reason to continue as though installation succeeded.

## 3. Distinguish an installed wrong version from a sufficient one

```bash
bash task.sh install-base --lab "$lab" --version 1.0
bash task.sh configure-app --lab "$lab"
printf 'CONFIGURE_STATUS=%s\n' "$?"
bash task.sh query --lab "$lab"
bash task.sh run --lab "$lab"
printf 'RUNTIME_STATUS=%s\n' "$?"
```

Base 1.0 can be installed successfully, while app configuration still fails
its `>= 2.0` requirement. The app remains unpacked. Its direct runtime check
separately rejects base 1.0 with status 2. Record those distinct statuses and
reasons. A dependency's name being present is not enough to satisfy a version
constraint. Do not edit the installed status database to make it look healthy.

## 4. Upgrade, check runtime, then configure and audit

```bash
bash task.sh install-base --lab "$lab" --version 2.0
bash task.sh query --lab "$lab"
bash task.sh run --lab "$lab"
bash task.sh configure-app --lab "$lab"
bash task.sh query --lab "$lab"
bash task.sh audit --lab "$lab"
bash task.sh run --lab "$lab"
```

Observe the app's actual database state before and after explicit
configuration. With base 2.0 the supplied program prints
`dependency-demo ready base=2.0` and exits 0, including before the app's
configuration step. That pre-configuration run deliberately demonstrates
that runtime success and fully installed metadata are different claims.
After configuration, require both packages to show `install ok installed`,
an empty consistency audit and another successful behavioral run.

These packages have no service unit or persistent service process. No service
restart or reboot is established by this experiment. A real patch plan must
identify such effects for the real application, preserve configuration/data,
retain recovery evidence and run its actual post-change acceptance check.

## 5. Observe dependent removal and cleanly undo the lab

Predict what should happen if the installed base is removed while the app
still depends on it. Then run and immediately retain the status:

```bash
bash task.sh remove-base --lab "$lab"
printf 'REMOVE_BASE_STATUS=%s\n' "$?"
bash task.sh query --lab "$lab"
bash task.sh run --lab "$lab"
bash task.sh remove-app --lab "$lab"
bash task.sh remove-base --lab "$lab"
bash task.sh audit --lab "$lab"
```

Require the first removal to fail without breaking the working installed
pair. The base can now show `deinstall ok installed`: its requested action
changed, while its current state and files remain installed. Read all three
status fields; the requested action does not prove removal. Remove the
dependent first, then the base. Verify the app and base
payload paths are gone and the separate database has no installed lab
packages. Record archive, dpkg-log and operation-log retention separately
from removal of installed payloads. Keep an outside sentinel unchanged.

Complete all five note sections with predictions and real query/audit/runtime
records. Preserve `dpkg.log` and `operations.jsonl`; the latter contains paired
command lifecycles, outputs and actual statuses. Repeat a changed sequence in
a fresh lab, such as installing base 2.0 before the app, and explain why its
first app install succeeds. Failed commands never become a success flag for
the whole investigation. After saving evidence, delete only the exact printed
disposable workspace and its own parent. Use the same numbered sequence for
independent study or pauses in an instructor walkthrough.

Primary references: [dpkg states and scoped installation options](https://manpages.debian.org/trixie/dpkg/dpkg.1.en.html)
and [Debian dependency metadata](https://www.debian.org/doc/manuals/debian-handbook/sect.package-meta-information.en.html).

# Dependency state and recovery: reference reasoning

Supply the current lab's actual output and statuses. This reference explains
relationships without pretending that a supplied run completes the record.

## 1. Predict and inspect package metadata

The app declares a base-version relationship. Building an archive does not
install it. The owned root has its own dpkg database, distinct from the host's
installed packages. All modification commands must identify that root.

## 2. Missing dependency

The initial app install unpacks files but cannot configure the package without
the base. Require the nonzero install status and observed unpacked state.
The actual runtime also fails because its needed file is missing. These are
separate observations; one diagnostic must not be replaced by empty success.

## 3. Wrong installed version

Base 1.0 can be fully installed while failing the app's `>= 2.0` relationship.
App configuration remains unsuccessful; the program separately rejects 1.0
with status 2. Merely finding a package by name cannot prove a versioned
dependency has been satisfied.

## 4. Upgrade, runtime and configuration

After installing base 2.0, observe the app state before explicitly configuring
it. Its runtime can now work while its database state remains unpacked.
Configure it, then require both installed states, an empty audit and another
behavioral run. Do not infer restart or reboot evidence for this stateless
demo. Actual applications may have those additional change requirements.

## 5. Removal, changed sequence and recovery limits

dpkg should refuse base removal while the configured app depends on it; the
pair should still work. Remove the app first, then the base. Require absent
payload files and no installed lab packages while preserving logs/archives.
Installing base 2.0 first should make the first app installation succeed in a
fresh lab. APT's repository dependency planning differs from dpkg installing
only supplied local archives. Neither a simulation nor package metadata alone
establishes a healthy real service after patching.

            os.killpg(child.pid, signal.SIGKILL)
            stdout, stderr = child.communicate()
        raise
    finally:
        record(root, dict(entry, event="end", endTime=time.time(), exitCode=child.returncode,
                          childProcessGroupCleanup=cleanup))
    record(root, dict(event="output", pid=child.pid, startTime=started,
                     status=child.returncode, stdout=stdout.decode(errors="replace"),
                     stderr=stderr.decode(errors="replace")))
    return child.returncode, stdout, stderr


def checked(root, argv):
    status, stdout, stderr = run(root, argv)
    if status:
        raise RuntimeError(f"command failed ({status}): {stderr.decode(errors='replace').strip()}")
    return stdout

# Interface, Route, Listener and Application Evidence

This required Unit 10 project replaces networking guesses with observations at
separate layers. Complete `network-notes.md` while retaining each raw JSON
record. The same prediction, observation and explanation pauses work for
independent reading and a paced walkthrough.

## Preparation and roles

Use an ordinary account in a Debian/Ubuntu Linux lab or WSL distribution.
The lab needs Python 3, Bash, iproute2 (`ip`, `ss`), iputils `ping`, and curl
7.76 or later. The DNS continuation also needs BIND `dig`. Arrange for these
tools to be available before the experiment. No Python packages are installed.
The website IDE edits, saves and exports these files; run the commands in the
external Linux lab after extracting the ZIP. The equipment rejects a non-Linux
host, root, non-loopback destinations and invalid port numbers.

Keep two terminals in the same selected role folder. `serve` occupies terminal A
and prints a ready record containing its actual address, port and PID. The
kernel selects an available port; never assume the example from another run.
Ctrl-C in that terminal closes the owned listener. `inspect` in terminal B
records actual commands, statuses, output, timestamps and process identities.
Use a new report name for each case. An existing report, including a symlink,
is preserved. A completed private report has mode 0600 and appears only after
all observations have been collected.

The collector returns 0 when the record was saved, including a recorded failed
request. That status is not a claim that the network is healthy or the worksheet
is complete. Read the request's `curlStatus`, `httpStatus`, body and error text.
Input or platform rejection returns 2; an equipment/report failure returns 1.
The starter and reference contain identical working equipment. Normal work is
the five named tasks in the notes, not rewriting the supplied Python services.
The reference explains a method; it cannot supply the current lab's live PIDs,
ports, paths, packet results or your initial prediction.

## Read the layers

An interface is a local network device; an address is assigned to an interface.
The `lo` loopback device carries traffic within this host. `ip -j address show
dev lo` records its flags and address/prefix entries. A loopback operstate of
UNKNOWN does not by itself mean that it is down. Read the flags and the actual
test too. The main route table and `ip -j route get 127.0.0.1` answer different
questions: configured main-table routes versus the kernel's selected local
path. A selected route describes a proposed path, not successful delivery.

A listening TCP socket has an address, port and owning process. `ss -H -ltnp`
lists listeners without name resolution and includes visible process ownership.
The supplied collector filters by the exact observed port. A healthy interface
and a successful ICMP echo do not prove that a particular TCP service is alive.
HTTP adds another layer: connecting to a server can still return a missing
path or an application failure.

## Predict, run and compare

1. Before starting a server, predict which layer names the address, route,
   listening process and application result. Record that prediction as task 1.
2. In terminal A run `bash task.sh serve`. Keep it running. Note the actual
   address, port and PID from its ready line.
3. In terminal B enter `read -r -p 'Port from the ready line: ' port`, then type
   that number. Run `bash task.sh inspect --port "$port" --report first.json`.
   Open `first.json`. Find the `lo` address, selected route, exact listener,
   ICMP observation, and HTTP status/body. `/health` returns 200 and a body
   containing `ready` and the server PID. Compare that PID with the ready line
   and `ss`; do not confuse the collector PID with the serving process.
4. Independently run `ip -j address show dev lo`, `ip -j route get 127.0.0.1`,
   `ss -H -ltnp "sport = :$port"`, and
   `curl --noproxy '*' --fail-with-body "http://127.0.0.1:$port/health"`.
   Compare these actual outputs with the corresponding saved observations.
5. Predict a request to an absent path, then run
   `bash task.sh inspect --port "$port" --path /missing --report missing.json`.
   Expect HTTP 404, curl status 22, and `missing` with the same server PID.
   This is an HTTP response from a listening server, not evidence of a dead port.
6. Stop terminal A with Ctrl-C. Confirm the exact listener is gone using `ss`.
   Run `bash task.sh inspect --port "$port" --report stopped.json`. In this
   controlled lab, expect curl status 7, HTTP status 000 (stored as integer 0),
   and no HTTP body. The interface/route may remain healthy. If another process
   has since acquired that port, record that actual observation instead of
   forcing the expected answer. Start a fresh owned server for another trial.
7. Start a fresh server, enter its new actual port and collect `restored.json`.
   Demonstrate HTTP 200 and the new listener PID. Preserve all earlier records.

The equipment disables curl proxies and uses literal 127.0.0.1/127.0.0.2 targets.
No public listener, route edit, firewall edit or internet request is needed.
An ICMP permission error in a restricted environment is an observation about
the available test, not proof that the HTTP service is down.

## Complete and retain

Finish all five notes tasks with an initial prediction, actual record/field
citations, your independent comparison, the stopped-service changed case, and
recovery/cleanup evidence. State the narrowest conclusion each tool supports.
Download/reopen the saved workspace and keep the reports with the final notes.
Running the reference does not complete the learner's investigation.

## Optional transfer

The listener continuation isolates wrong bind addresses, absent paths and
application readiness. The DNS continuation deliberately separates a DNS answer
from an explicit HTTP address override. These are distinct optional experiments
after this core checkpoint, not three copies of one log-summary script.

Primary references: [ip](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/ip.8.html),
[ss](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/ss.8.html),
[ping](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/ping.8.html), and
[curl options and exit codes](https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html).

# Listener Failure versus an HTTP Error

This optional transfer follows the required interface/route investigation.
Keep the same local path while changing one service property at a time.
Complete `listener-notes.md`; do not replace evidence with a generic list of
networking commands or change the host's networking configuration.

## Equipment and recording

Use an ordinary account in a Debian/Ubuntu Linux lab or WSL distribution.
The lab needs Python 3, Bash, iproute2 (`ip`, `ss`), iputils `ping`, and curl
7.76 or later. The DNS continuation also needs BIND `dig`. Arrange for these
tools to be available before the experiment. No Python packages are installed.
The website IDE edits, saves and exports these files; run the commands in the
external Linux lab after extracting the ZIP. The equipment rejects a non-Linux
host, root, non-loopback destinations and invalid port numbers.

Keep two terminals in the same selected role folder. `serve` occupies terminal A
and prints a ready record containing its actual address, port and PID. The
kernel selects an available port; never assume the example from another run.
Ctrl-C in that terminal closes the owned listener. `inspect` in terminal B
records actual commands, statuses, output, timestamps and process identities.
Use a new report name for each case. An existing report, including a symlink,
is preserved. A completed private report has mode 0600 and appears only after
all observations have been collected.

The collector returns 0 when the record was saved, including a recorded failed
request. That status is not a claim that the network is healthy or the worksheet
is complete. Read the request's `curlStatus`, `httpStatus`, body and error text.

The starter and reference contain identical working equipment. Normal work is
the five named tasks in the notes, not rewriting the supplied Python services.
The reference explains a method; it cannot supply the current lab's live PIDs,
ports, paths, packet results or your initial prediction.

## Distinguish the cases before running them

The bind address belongs to the listening socket. A connection aimed at
127.0.0.1 does not reach a socket bound only to 127.0.0.2, even when the numeric
port is equal. Linux normally routes both through loopback. Compare the exact
local address in `ss`, the selected destination, and the owning PID before
guessing a missing route or firewall rule. `ping` tests ICMP, not that TCP port.

The supplied HTTP service has two modes. Ready mode returns 200 at `/health`;
unavailable mode returns 503 there. Both return 404 for `/missing`. Every body
includes the actual serving PID. With `--fail-with-body`, curl retains 4xx/5xx
bodies but returns 22. A refused TCP connection instead has curl status 7 and
no HTTP response. The collector saves these distinct outcomes without turning
them into a fabricated all-pass summary.

## Controlled sequence

1. In notes task 1, predict the first failing layer and expected `ss`, curl
   status and HTTP status for each case below. Keep your initial prediction.
2. Terminal A: `bash task.sh serve --bind 127.0.0.2`. In terminal B enter
   `read -r -p 'Port from the ready line: ' port`. Then run
   `bash task.sh inspect --port "$port" --address 127.0.0.1 --report wrong-bind.json`.
   The listener exists at .2, while this request targets .1. Identify that
   mismatch using actual addresses rather than calling every failed request DNS.
3. With that same server still running, use
   `bash task.sh inspect --port "$port" --address 127.0.0.2 --report changed-target.json`.
   Expect HTTP 200. Explain why this diagnostic client change proves a reachable
   endpoint but does not move the server's bind address.
4. Stop the .2 server. Start `bash task.sh serve --bind 127.0.0.1` and enter its
   actual new port. Save `ready.json`, then run
   `bash task.sh inspect --port "$port" --path /missing --report missing-path.json`.
   Compare HTTP 200 at `/health` with 404 at `/missing`, the retained body and
   the same listening process. A missing URL is not a missing TCP listener.
5. Stop the server. Start `bash task.sh serve --mode unavailable`, enter its
   port and save `unavailable.json`. The expected result is HTTP 503 with curl
   status 22 and an `unavailable` body. The process and socket still exist.
   State what this controlled fixture proves and what a real 503 would still
   require examining, such as application dependencies and its own logs.
6. Stop that server, start ready mode again and save `recovered.json` using the
   new port. Independently verify the exact listener/PID with
   `ss -H -ltnp "sport = :$port"` and request `/health` using curl. Finally stop
   it and verify the owned listener disappears. Keep all case records.

## Explain the repair

Complete the five notes tasks: predictions, bind mismatch evidence and changed
target, path comparison, application readiness, and recovery/cleanup. State
which correction belongs to the client destination, listening configuration,
URL path or application behavior. The reference describes these relationships
without inventing a server PID or treating every HTTP error as a network outage.
Normal completion requires the actual changed cases and a corrected local
request. No proxy, system service, firewall or public exposure is introduced.

Primary references: [ss socket filters](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/ss.8.html)
and [curl error/body behavior](https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html).

# Controlled DNS Diagnosis and Explicit Address Bypass

This optional extension separates a DNS answer, an address selection and an
HTTP request. Complete `resolver-notes.md` after the core networking checkpoint.
The supplied DNS implementation is complete equipment, not a request to write
a recursive resolver or replace the host's resolver configuration.

## Preparation and processes

Use an ordinary account in a Debian/Ubuntu Linux lab or WSL distribution.
The lab needs Python 3, Bash, iproute2 (`ip`, `ss`), iputils `ping`, and curl
7.76 or later. The DNS continuation also needs BIND `dig`. Arrange for these
tools to be available before the experiment. No Python packages are installed.
The website IDE edits, saves and exports these files; run the commands in the
external Linux lab after extracting the ZIP. The equipment rejects a non-Linux
host, root, non-loopback destinations and invalid port numbers.

Keep two terminals in the same selected role folder. `serve` occupies terminal A
and prints a ready record containing its actual address, port and PID. The
kernel selects an available port; never assume the example from another run.
Ctrl-C in that terminal closes the owned listener. `inspect` in terminal B
records actual commands, statuses, output, timestamps and process identities.
Use a new report name for each case. An existing report, including a symlink,
is preserved. A completed private report has mode 0600 and appears only after
all observations have been collected.

The collector returns 0 when the record was saved, including a recorded failed
request. That status is not a claim that the network is healthy or the worksheet
is complete. Read the request's `curlStatus`, `httpStatus`, body and error text.
Input or platform rejection returns 2; an equipment/report failure returns 1.
The starter and reference contain identical working equipment. Normal work is
the five named tasks in the notes, not rewriting the supplied Python services.
The reference explains a method; it cannot supply the current lab's live PIDs,
ports, paths, packet results or your initial prediction.

Use three terminals in the selected role folder. Terminal A runs HTTP:
`bash task.sh serve`. Terminal B runs the controlled DNS service:
`bash task.sh dns --answer ready`. Both print independently selected ports and
PIDs. In terminal C enter `read -r -p 'HTTP port: ' http_port` and
`read -r -p 'DNS port: ' dns_port` using those actual ready lines. The DNS
fixture listens only on 127.0.0.1 UDP at its unprivileged port, not public port
53. It answers a single ordinary IN/A question for `lab.invalid.` with TTL 0.
The supported diagnostic uses UDP with EDNS and recursion disabled. This small
fixture does not implement general recursion, caching, TCP fallback or DNSSEC.

## Predict and separate observations

1. Predict how a valid address, an incorrect address and NXDOMAIN should differ
   in the DNS record and the later HTTP request. Record the prediction first.
2. With ready DNS running, use
   `bash task.sh inspect --dns-port "$dns_port" --http-port "$http_port" --report ready.json`.
   Find DNS status NOERROR, one A answer 127.0.0.1, the actual UDP listener PID,
   the HTTP listener PID, and HTTP 200. Independently inspect the answer using
   `dig -r @127.0.0.1 -p "$dns_port" lab.invalid. A +noedns +norecurse +notcp +nosearch +time=1 +tries=1`.
   An explicit server/port and final dot make this a query of the owned fixture;
   it does not test the host's ordinary name-service search path.
3. Leave HTTP running. Stop only terminal B and restart DNS with
   `bash task.sh dns --answer wrong`. Enter its new DNS port in terminal C and
   collect `wrong-answer.json`. NOERROR now supplies 127.0.0.2. The request
   following that selected answer should fail to connect to the .1 HTTP
   listener, while `explicitBypassRequest` still returns 200 at .1. Cite both
   results. DNS query success alone does not prove that its answer is correct.
4. Stop only DNS, restart `bash task.sh dns --answer missing`, enter its actual
   port and collect `nxdomain.json`. The DNS response says NXDOMAIN. `dig` can
   exit 0 for this valid negative response. The collector does not attempt the
   selected-address HTTP request because no A answer exists; that field is null.
   It separately performs the explicit .1 bypass to test the unchanged app.
5. Restore DNS using `--answer ready`, enter the new DNS port and collect
   `restored.json`. Independently query that server again and verify the ready
   answer plus a successful selected-address HTTP request. Stop both foreground
   servers, and use `ss -H -lunp "sport = :$dns_port"` and
   `ss -H -ltnp "sport = :$http_port"` to confirm their owned sockets are gone.

## What the bypass does

For the HTTP experiment the collector supplies the observed fixture address
to curl's `--resolve lab.invalid:PORT:ADDRESS`, with proxies disabled. Curl
therefore uses the explicit address for that one host/port pair. This makes
the relationship between the captured DNS answer and connection test visible;
it does not route curl's DNS lookups through the fixture automatically.
The separate .1 override can demonstrate a healthy app despite bad/missing
DNS, but is not evidence that the system resolver was repaired. This exercise
does not edit `/etc/hosts`, `/etc/resolv.conf`, routes, firewall rules or global
DNS. The repair being demonstrated is the owned DNS fixture's restored answer.

## Complete and retain

Finish the five notes tasks with the original prediction, independent DNS
comparison, incorrect-answer case, negative-answer case and restored/cleaned
state. Identify both process PIDs and both ports from actual records. Keep
claims about global resolution, TCP service reachability and HTTP status
separate. Reopen the saved workspace and retain all four reports with the notes.

Primary references: [BIND dig](https://bind9.readthedocs.io/en/latest/manpages.html#dig-dns-lookup-utility),
[curl --resolve](https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html#--resolve), and
[RFC 1035](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035.html) for the restricted
DNS packet equipment.

README.md.content:
# Capacity Evidence, Verified Backup and Separate Restore

This is the required Unit 12 project. Investigate actual capacity and a separate verified restoration before optional continuations. The notebook continues the same core attempt.

## Environment and saved work

Use an ordinary account in a Debian/Ubuntu Linux lab or WSL distribution with
Python 3, Bash, GNU tar and GNU coreutils (`df`, `du`, `sha256sum`). Arrange for
missing tools before starting. No package installation is part of this lab.
The site IDE edits, saves and exports these sources and notes. Confirm the
selected role's import, download its ZIP, extract it and run commands from the
role folder in the external Linux terminal. Browser saving does not run tar.

The starter and reference have identical working equipment. Complete the five
named tasks in the notes using predictions and actual evidence; the reference
explains a method without fabricating this lab's paths, sizes, timings or hashes.
Use the same numbered pauses for independent reading and a paced walkthrough.
An equipment exit of 0 does not complete the notes. Errors are separate: invalid
arguments, root, the wrong platform, an existing name or a stale policy return
2; missing tools, failed native commands or corrupt backup evidence return 1.
An ordinary handled interruption returns 130.

Start with a fresh private parent and keep this shell open:

```bash
uname -s
id -u
python3 --version
tar --version
df --version
lab_parent=$(mktemp -d)
lab="$lab_parent/storage"
bash task.sh init --lab "$lab"
```

Record the exact printed absolute `lab` path. Initialization refuses an existing
path. All commands require this account's matching lab marker and regular files
or directories. Keep this directory private; do not substitute real home,
shared, system or production data. The small supplied dataset has a text
version, a binary file, a filename containing a space, an empty directory, a
1 MiB sparse file and an explicitly excluded transient `cache` directory.

The archive contains `data` contents except `cache`. Its manifest records file
names, types, content hashes, sizes, account ownership and permission modes,
plus archive SHA-256, sequence, source path and the capacity observation.
`backup` first checks currently available bytes against apparent input size,
archive overhead and a configurable reserve (16 MiB by default). Space can
change after that check. The actual tar status and complete inventory check
remain necessary. A partial staging directory is discarded after a handled
command failure or interruption; earlier published backups remain in place.
A power loss or SIGKILL can leave staging evidence, which requires inspection.
It never counts as a valid backup.

Archive checks reject unsupported paths, links, special files, extra/missing
members, content mismatches and special permission bits. Restore uses actual
GNU tar only after validation, into a new directory under `restores`. It
refuses an existing destination and compares restored bytes, paths, ownership
and modes with the saved inventory. The original source is checked separately.
Failures do not become empty successful summaries.

Commands, PIDs, start/end times, statuses, stdout, stderr and child cleanup are
retained in private `operations.jsonl`. Keep that record with the notes, source
observations, manifests, trusted checksum record and restored comparison.

## Scope of the evidence

`df` observes the containing mounted filesystem. `du` observes the selected tree;
its apparent-size mode counts logical lengths rather than allocated blocks.

bytes. Read actual results instead of assuming the two totals match. Inode
availability is another resource, separate from available bytes. The plain tar
archive need not preserve the original sparse allocation, even when restored
content and length match.

These owned archives use the same filesystem as the source. They demonstrate
file recovery, not survival of that disk's failure. A real backup plan needs
an independently protected copy, explicit recovery point/time requirements,
access control and repeated restoration tests. RAID, replication and a copied
file alone do not establish that recovery requirement. The manifest here is
an integrity reference, not a signature: changing both archive and manifest
can defeat a self-contained checksum claim. Retain a trusted checksum record
separately. This regular-file lab does not establish database consistency or
preservation of ACLs, xattrs, links, device files or a bootable system.

length and inode availability. Run `bash task.sh observe --lab "$lab" --report
first` and open `reports/first.json`. The four recorded commands are actual df
and du queries. Independently repeat the displayed commands and compare their
scope, units and current output. Read `sparseFile.size` and `allocatedBytes`.
Record actual mount identity, available bytes and inodes; do not invent totals.
Reusing `--report first` refuses replacement and preserves its original bytes.

## 2. Create and independently inspect a backup

```bash

bash task.sh list --lab "$lab" --name initial
bash task.sh verify --lab "$lab" --name initial
sha256sum -- "$lab/backups/initial/archive.tar"
```

file, the empty directory and its mode; confirm `cache` is absent from the
archive while its source file still exists. A listing proves readable archive
structure, while verification also checks content and the declared member set.
Keep this initial backup and manifest. An existing backup name is refused.

## 3. Change live data, then restore the earlier state separately

```bash

```

restore destination and retain its refusal plus unchanged restored bytes.

actual restore evidence. The troubleshooting notebook continues this same
attempt rather than creating another program.

selected role's import, download its ZIP, extract it and run commands from the
role folder in the external Linux terminal. Browser saving does not run tar.

named tasks in the notes using predictions and actual evidence; the reference
explains a method without fabricating this lab's paths, sizes, timings or hashes.
Use the same numbered pauses for independent reading and a paced walkthrough.
An equipment exit of 0 does not complete the notes. Errors are separate: invalid
arguments, root, the wrong platform, an existing name or a stale policy return
2; missing tools, failed native commands or corrupt backup evidence return 1.

Start with a fresh private parent and keep this shell open:

```bash
uname -s
id -u
python3 --version
tar --version
df --version
lab_parent=$(mktemp -d)
lab="$lab_parent/storage"
bash task.sh init --lab "$lab"
```

path. All commands require this account's matching lab marker and regular files
or directories. Keep this directory private; do not substitute real home,
shared, system or production data. The small supplied dataset has a text
version, a binary file, a filename containing a space, an empty directory, a
1 MiB sparse file and an explicitly excluded transient `cache` directory.

names, types, content hashes, sizes, account ownership and permission modes,

change after that check. The actual tar status and complete inventory check
remain necessary. A partial staging directory is discarded after a handled
command failure or interruption; earlier published backups remain in place.

It never counts as a valid backup.

members, content mismatches and special permission bits. Restore uses actual
GNU tar only after validation, into a new directory under `restores`. It

## 1. Establish a trustworthy comparison

does and does not prove. Run:

```bash
bash task.sh backup --lab "$lab" --name baseline
bash task.sh list --lab "$lab" --name baseline
bash task.sh verify --lab "$lab" --name baseline
bash task.sh restore --lab "$lab" --name baseline --destination trusted-copy
sha256sum -- "$lab/backups/baseline/archive.tar"
```

Save the actual manifest/checksum outside
the archive and compare every restored entry. Keep this good backup untouched.

## 2. Change content without breaking the tar listing

```bash
bash task.sh backup --lab "$lab" --name damaged
bash task.sh damage --lab "$lab" --name damaged --mode flip
bash task.sh list --lab "$lab" --name damaged
bash task.sh verify --lab "$lab" --name damaged

```

and names remain readable. Expect a successful listing but a nonzero integrity
check (1). Compare the changed archive SHA-256 with its retained manifest.
Do not rewrite the manifest to manufacture a pass. This controlled fault
explains why archive readability alone does not prove correct backup content.

was never created, live data is unchanged and the trusted baseline and restore

statuses rather than treating a tar diagnostic as a completed investigation.


mode and current account with the new manifest and source. The repaired backup
is a new artifact; it does not repair the damaged historical bytes. Preserve
both failed records and the original good baseline. Complete all five notes
with initial predictions, independent checksum/listing results, refusal before
destination creation, changed-case evidence and recovery/cleanup observations.

README.md.content:
# Literal Search, Filename Boundaries and Three Outcomes

This optional transfer follows the required structured log-summary project.
It returns the names of text files containing a literal string. It does not
count severity fields, recursively discover files or edit input data. The
new work is a filename pipeline and the distinction between matches, no
matches and a failed search. Complete `search-notes.md` with actual evidence.
The prediction, inspection and explanation pauses support independent study
and a paced walkthrough.

## Equipment and stream contract

Use an ordinary account in an owned Linux lab with Bash, GNU grep and GNU sort.
Extract one role with its `records` folder. The site IDE edits, saves and exports
the workspace; run these commands in the external Linux lab after extraction.
No installation, system configuration or privileged access is part of the task.

`task.sh` accepts a nonempty literal string and one or more explicit ordinary
nonsymlink text-file paths. Each shell argument remains one filename. Quote
spaces, wildcard characters and newlines. The script rejects a standalone `-`
operand, directories, symbolic links and special files. A nonexistent or
unreadable file reaches grep and produces an actual tool error.

The pipeline is `grep -F -l -Z -e TEXT -- FILE... | sort -z -u`. `-F` interprets
text literally; `-e` protects a pattern beginning with a dash, and `--` ends
option parsing for the file operands. `-l` selects filenames rather than lines.
`-Z` terminates each filename with NUL; `sort -z -u` preserves that separator,
sorts the byte strings under the script's C locale, and removes repeated
identical path arguments. NUL cannot occur inside a Unix filename, while a
newline can. This does not merge different paths that happen to name the same
underlying file. Do not store a NUL stream in shell command substitution.

The reference returns 0 when at least one file matches and both tools succeed,
1 when no file matches and sorting succeeds, and 2 for invalid arguments or a
tool failure. stderr separately reports `grep=N sort=N`. stdout can contain
some valid names before an input fails. Status 2 makes that list incomplete;
discard it as a complete result. `grep -q` is deliberately absent because its
early success can conceal an error after a match.

## Predict, run and inspect the filename stream

From the selected role folder, predict the literal matches for `ERROR[42]`.
The supplied `alpha.txt` and `-dash.txt` contain that exact byte string;
`with space.txt` contains `ERROR4`, which is different literal text.

~~~bash

search_status=$?
printf 'status=%s\n' "$search_status"
cat first.err
while IFS= read -r -d '' file; do printf '%q\n' "$file"; done < first.bin
~~~

In the unfinished starter, the search and sort already run, but the final
status interpretation is the named TODO and always returns 2. Complete the
last decision using both saved array entries. A grep status of 1 is a valid
no-match outcome, while any nonzero sort status and a grep status greater
than 1 are failures. Keep the NUL separator, literal matching and input guards.
Compare the reference after recording a working attempt.

`PIPESTATUS` belongs to Bash and is replaced by the next foreground command,
even a diagnostic print. The assignment immediately after the pipeline saves
both original entries. `set +e` prevents an ordinary no-match status from
ending the script before that assignment; `set -e` is restored afterward.
`pipefail` alone supplies one aggregate status and cannot explain which tool
failed. Never add `|| true` and then report the search as successful.

against all three supplied files: expect an empty NUL stream and status 1 in

owned lab; restore its original mode afterward. An empty list does not by
itself distinguish no matches from a failed search. Reopen the saved workspace
and retain the five completed notes tasks; a reference run does not complete

README.md.content:
# Partial Input, Pipeline Statuses and Misleading Success

This optional extension follows the required log-summary project. It keeps a
small two-stage pipeline visible: cat reads explicit text files, and awk counts
exact level fields. The investigation is whether a printed summary proves that
all input was read. Complete `pipeline-notes.md` using predictions and actual
stdout, stderr and both stage statuses. The same pauses support independent
reading and a paced walkthrough.

## Equipment and contract

Use an ordinary account in an owned Linux lab with Bash, cat and awk. Extract
one role with `count.awk` and the complete `records` folder. The website IDE
supports editing, saving and ZIP export; execute the pipeline in that external
Linux lab. The program changes no inputs, permissions or system configuration.

`bash task.sh FILE...` accepts one or more ordinary nonsymlink text-file paths.
A standalone `-`, a directory, a symbolic link or a special file is rejected.
A missing or unreadable path reaches the actual cat command and yields an input
failure. Quote each path; each operand is resolved from the caller's working
directory. The supplied awk program is located beside `task.sh`, even when the
script is invoked through an absolute path from another directory.

The input format has a timestamp in field one, a level in field two and then a
message. `count.awk` counts only exact ERROR and WARNING level fields. An INFO
message containing ERROR contributes neither an error nor a warning. `ERROR[42]`
is also a different level. On all three supplied files the complete result is
`errors=2 warnings=2`. Empty successful input gives two zero counts.

Every run prints `producer=N consumer=N` to stderr after immediately saving
Bash's `PIPESTATUS`. In the reference, status 0 means both cat and awk exited 0;
status 2 means invalid arguments or either stage failed. A printed summary
on status 2 is partial or unavailable, not a complete count. It is retained
for diagnosis, not hidden or replaced with invented zeroes.

## Healthy prediction and the intentionally misleading starter

From the selected role folder:

~~~bash
bash task.sh records/alpha.txt 'records/with space.txt' records/-dash.txt > healthy.txt 2> healthy.err
pipeline_status=$?
printf 'status=%s\n' "$pipeline_status"
cat healthy.txt
cat healthy.err
~~~

The unmodified starter succeeds here because its named TODO checks only awk.
Its defect becomes visible when cat reads one valid file and then fails to read
another. Predict the partial counts before running this changed case:

~~~bash
bash task.sh records/alpha.txt records/absent.txt > partial.txt 2> partial.err
pipeline_status=$?
printf 'status=%s\n' "$pipeline_status"
cat partial.txt
cat partial.err
~~~

With `absent.txt` genuinely absent, cat exits nonzero after the valid first
file; awk still reaches its normal END block and prints `errors=1 warnings=1`.
The starter returns 0 because it ignores cat's saved status. Correct the named
condition to include both original array entries. The completed implementation
returns 2 for this run. Preserve the partial output and actual diagnostics, then
explain why neither a printed number nor a successful final stage proves that
all input was available. Compare the reference after completing that repair.

## Why the status capture is placed there

By default a pipeline's status is its last command's status. `set -o pipefail`
changes that aggregate to the rightmost nonzero status, but it does not identify
all stage outcomes. `PIPESTATUS` records the separate stage results. The next
foreground command replaces it, so the array assignment immediately follows
the pipeline. With `errexit` enabled a failing pipeline can stop the script
before evidence is collected. The program uses `set +e` only around this
observation and restores `set -e` after saving the array. It then makes an
explicit final decision. Do not move a print, assignment to another variable,
or `|| true` between the pipeline and the array capture.

## Independent cases, consumer failure and restoration

Create an empty ordinary text file, run it as the sole input, and observe status
0 with both zero counts after the repair. Copy `alpha.txt` to a filename with
spaces and confirm that quoting keeps it one argument. Record what happens
when a valid input follows a missing one; incomplete input remains a failure
regardless of order.

In a disposable copy of the extracted role, preserve `count.awk` before making
its syntax invalid. Append an unclosed BEGIN block, run one supplied input,
then restore the exact original awk file:

~~~bash
cp count.awk count.awk.original
printf '\nBEGIN {\n' >> count.awk
bash task.sh records/alpha.txt > consumer.txt 2> consumer.err
pipeline_status=$?
printf 'status=%s\n' "$pipeline_status"
cat consumer.err
mv -- count.awk.original count.awk
bash task.sh records/alpha.txt > restored.txt 2> restored.err
restored_status=$?
printf 'restored=%s\n' "$restored_status"
~~~

The actual awk syntax error makes the consumer nonzero. Cat can either finish
its small write before that failure or receive SIGPIPE; record the observed
producer status instead of assuming a particular ordering. The reference and
completed starter return 2 either way. Restoring the original awk program and
rerunning the same input demonstrates recovery. The valid one-file summary is
`errors=1 warnings=1`.

Retain five completed notes tasks, the changed-case outputs, the actual input
failure and consumer-failure diagnostics, and the restored result. Remove only
the disposable test files created in the selected role folder. Reopen the saved
workspace and explain the repair before comparing the reference. A successful
reference run does not complete the learner's evidence record.

Primary references: [Bash pipelines](https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/html_node/Pipelines),
[Bash PIPESTATUS](https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/html_node/Bash-Variables.html),
and [GNU awk records and fields](https://www.gnu.org/software/gawk/manual/html_node/Fields.html).

# Logical Paths, Physical Targets and Parent Traversal This optional transfer follows the directory-purpose and static-site project. A path used by a service or shell can include a symbolic link. Its visible name, resolved target and parent traversal are separate observations. The project reports those paths; it does not serve files, install a release, change permissions or prove that a service is configured correctly. Complete `path-notes.md` with predictions and actual results. The same pauses support independent study and a paced walkthrough. ## Concepts and equipment Use an ordinary account in an owned Linux lab with Bash. The site IDE edits, saves and exports the source; execute these commands in the external Linux terminal after extraction. The supplied program is read-only. The following commands create a disposable directory/link example under one private parent. They do not change `/srv`, `/etc`, `/var`, `/usr` or system configuration. A symbolic link stores another path. A relative link target is interpreted from the link's containing directory. Bash's logical directory mode retains the traversed link spelling in PWD, while physical mode resolves the actual directory. In logical mode `..` removes the last logical path component; in physical mode it moves to the resolved directory's parent. These can differ. Neither visible directory spelling nor an `ls` listing alone proves the target that another program will open. ## Create a real link and predict the four paths From the extracted role folder, retain the printed parent path in this shell: ~~~bash lab_root=$(mktemp -d) printf 'lab_root=%s\n' "$lab_root" mkdir -p "$lab_root/physical/site" printf '

Owned example

\n' > "$lab_root/physical/site/index.html" ln -s physical/site "$lab_root/served" readlink -- "$lab_root/served" ~~~ Predict these four values: logical directory, resolved physical directory, logical parent and physical parent. For this arrangement the logical path ends in `/served`, the physical path ends in `/physical/site`, the logical parent is the private parent, and the physical parent ends in `/physical`. The absolute prefix comes from this run; it is not supplied as an observation. ~~~bash bash task.sh "$lab_root/served" > linked.paths 2> linked.err trace_status=$? printf 'status=%s\n' "$trace_status" cat linked.err while IFS= read -r -d '' field && IFS= read -r -d '' value; do printf '%s=%q\n' "$field" "$value" done < linked.paths ~~~ The output is four field/value pairs, each separated by NUL. NUL cannot occur inside a Unix path, while spaces and newlines can. The display loop quotes each value for inspection without splitting it. Keep the binary record alongside its decoded display. Do not use command substitution to store a NUL stream. Independently compare Bash's own directory observations in a child shell: ~~~bash ( cd -L -- "$lab_root/served" pwd -L pwd -P (cd -L -- .. && pwd -L) (cd -P -- .. && pwd -P) ) ~~~ The four printed lines correspond to the four recorded fields for this ordinary path arrangement. The binary program output also preserves paths containing newlines, which plain line output cannot label unambiguously. The starter deliberately computes the field named physical_parent using logical traversal at its single TODO. Repair that flag so the field describes the physical parent. Keep the other three observations, argument boundary and binary stream unchanged. Compare the reference after recording a working attempt. Status 0 means all four observations completed; it does not mean the starter's named decision is repaired or the worksheet is complete. Status 2 means invalid input or an unsupported environment, and a failed directory change can return 1. Discard a partial record as a complete result. ## Compare direct access and another logical spelling ~~~bash bash task.sh "$lab_root/physical/site" > direct.paths 2> direct.err ln -s physical/site "$lab_root/another view" bash task.sh "$lab_root/another view" > alternate.paths 2> alternate.err ~~~ The two link spellings have different logical paths and the same physical path. Direct access has the same logical and physical directory. Record each run's status and decode its record independently. Verify the document remains unchanged. A `cd` inside the program runs in a child shell and does not change the caller's working directory. For a changed case, create a failed target and then correct that exact link: ~~~bash ln -s missing-target "$lab_root/broken" bash task.sh "$lab_root/broken" > broken.paths 2> broken.err broken_status=$? printf 'broken=%s\n' "$broken_status" rm -- "$lab_root/broken" ln -s physical/site "$lab_root/broken" bash task.sh "$lab_root/broken" > corrected.paths 2> corrected.err corrected_status=$? printf 'corrected=%s\n' "$corrected_status" external_root=$(mktemp -d) printf 'external_root=%s\n' "$external_root" mkdir -- "$external_root/target" ln -s "$external_root/target" "$lab_root/outside view" bash task.sh "$lab_root/outside view" > outside.paths 2> outside.err ~~~ Record how a name inside the first tree resolves outside that tree. The program reports the selected readable path and does not enforce containment. This is a path-observation exercise, not a deployment or access-control check. No arbitrary production path is needed for the experiment. ## Retain evidence and clean up Complete the five notes tasks with the predicted and actual paths, the TODO repair, direct/alternate comparisons, failed target and corrected target. Verify the source bytes, current identity and caller directory remain as recorded. Remove the exact disposable directories after reviewing their printed values; keep the saved workspace and result records separately. ~~~bash printf 'Review before removal: %q\n' "$lab_root" "$external_root" rm -r -- "$lab_root" "$external_root" ~~~ Primary references: [Bash cd modes](https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/html_node/Bourne-Shell-Builtins.html) and [GNU symbolic links](https://www.gnu.org/s/coreutils/manual/html_node/ln-invocation.html).

# Reported Size, Read Bytes and Live Kernel Files

This optional extension distinguishes a file's metadata, its mounted
filesystem and bytes returned by a real read. Linux kernel views such as
`/proc/uptime` are generated information, not ordinary stored documents.
Complete `filesystem-notes.md` with actual observations. The prediction,
inspection and explanation pauses support independent study and a paced
walkthrough. This is separate from the core static-site deployment and from
later disk-capacity, archive and restore investigations.

## Equipment and what the program measures

Use an ordinary account in an owned Linux lab with Python 3.8 or later, Bash, GNU stat,
GNU head and util-linux findmnt. Preserve `filesystem_observer.py` beside
`task.sh` when extracting the role. The website IDE edits, saves and exports
these files; it does not provide the Linux kernel observations.

The program accepts one or more explicit paths. It resolves symbolic links,
rejects directories, FIFOs, devices and a standalone `-`, and reads only
regular files or readable regular-looking kernel pseudo-files. It never
writes to the selected inputs, changes mount configuration or invokes sudo.
Each path is inspected by actual `stat`, `findmnt` and `head` commands, with
separate arguments, bounded subprocess time and retained statuses/output.

`stat` reports metadata size, device and inode. `findmnt --target` identifies
the path's actual mounted filesystem; the program explicitly requests JSON
TARGET, FSTYPE and SOURCE columns. A directory name is not enough to identify
that filesystem. `head` reads at most 4097 bytes. The report retains a maximum
4096-byte base64 capture plus its SHA-256, records the actual bytes returned,
and marks truncated captures. A large file's size can exceed that bounded
read without being a kernel view. Metadata and content are observed by
separate commands, so a changing input is not one atomic snapshot.

## Predict ordinary, empty and kernel-backed observations

Create two ordinary inputs under a private disposable directory. Keep the
printed parent path for this shell:

~~~bash
lab_root=$(mktemp -d)
printf 'lab_root=%s\n' "$lab_root"
printf 'alpha\n' > "$lab_root/ordinary.txt"
: > "$lab_root/empty.txt"
~~~

"""Observe actual file metadata, mounted filesystem and a bounded byte read."""
import argparse
import base64
import datetime
import hashlib
import json
import os
import platform
import signal
import stat
import subprocess
import sys
import time
from pathlib import Path

LIMIT = 4096
commands = []
completed = []


class ToolFailure(Exception):
    pass


def content_is_empty(reported_size, observed_bytes):
    return reported_size == 0 # TODO: use the count from the actual successful read.


def tool(argv):
    child = subprocess.Popen(argv, stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL, stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
                             stderr=subprocess.PIPE, start_new_session=True,
                             env=dict(os.environ, LC_ALL="C"))
    entry = {"parentTaskId": os.environ.get("CLASSES_FAMILY_TASK_ID", "filesystem-observation"),
             "parentPid": os.getpid(), "command": argv, "cwd": os.getcwd(), "pid": child.pid,
             "startTime": time.time(), "timeoutSeconds": 15}
    cleanup = "owned process exited and reaped"
    out, err = b"", b""
    timed_out = False
    try:
        out, err = child.communicate(timeout=15)
    except BaseException as error:
        cleanup = "owned process group terminated after timeout or interruption"
        if child.poll() is None:
            try:
                os.killpg(child.pid, signal.SIGTERM)
            except ProcessLookupError:
                pass
        try:
            out, err = child.communicate(timeout=2)
        except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
            os.killpg(child.pid, signal.SIGKILL)
            out, err = child.communicate()
        if isinstance(error, subprocess.TimeoutExpired):
            timed_out = True
        else:
            raise
    finally:
        entry.update({"endTime": time.time(), "exitCode": child.returncode,
                      "childProcessGroupCleanup": cleanup, "timedOut": timed_out,
                      "stdoutBase64": base64.b64encode(out).decode(),
                      "stderr": err.decode(errors="replace")})
        commands.append(entry)
    if timed_out:
        raise ToolFailure("A native command timed out; no complete result is available.")
    if child.returncode:
        raise ToolFailure("A native observation command failed; no complete result is available.")
    return out


def observe(value):
    if value == "-":
        raise ValueError("A path cannot select standard input (-).")
    path = Path(value).resolve(strict=True)
    if not stat.S_ISREG(path.stat().st_mode):
        raise ValueError("Use a regular file or a readable kernel pseudo-file.")
    raw = tool(["stat", "-L", "--printf=%s:%d:%i", "--", str(path)]).decode()
    size, device, inode = map(int, raw.split(":"))
    mounts = json.loads(tool(["findmnt", "--json", "--target", str(path),
                              "--output", "TARGET,FSTYPE,SOURCE"]))["filesystems"]
    if len(mounts) != 1:
        raise ValueError("The selected path did not produce one actual mount record.")
    data = tool(["head", "--bytes=" + str(LIMIT + 1), "--", str(path)])
    return {"inputPath": value, "resolvedPath": str(path),
            "reportedSize": size, "device": device, "inode": inode,
            "filesystem": mounts[0], "bytesRead": len(data), "captureLimit": LIMIT,
            "truncated": len(data) > LIMIT,
            "capturedBase64": base64.b64encode(data[:LIMIT]).decode(),
            "capturedSha256": hashlib.sha256(data[:LIMIT]).hexdigest(),
            "contentEmpty": content_is_empty(size, len(data)),
            "observedAt": datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).isoformat()}


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("paths", nargs="+")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    if platform.system() != "Linux" or os.geteuid() == 0:
        raise ValueError("Use an ordinary account in an owned Linux lab.")
    for value in args.paths:
        completed.append(observe(value))
    print(json.dumps({"observationsCompleted": True, "observations": completed,
                      "commands": commands, "learnerWorksheetCompletionInferred": False},
                     indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    try:
        main()
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        print(json.dumps({"error": "Interrupted", "completed": completed,
                          "commands": commands}), file=sys.stderr)
        raise SystemExit(130)
    except ToolFailure as error:
        print(json.dumps({"error": str(error), "completed": completed,
                          "commands": commands}), file=sys.stderr)
        raise SystemExit(1)
    except (ValueError, OSError) as error:
        print(json.dumps({"error": str(error), "completed": completed,
                          "commands": commands}), file=sys.stderr)
        raise SystemExit(2)

README.md.content:
# Deleting Names and Writing File Contents

This optional transfer follows the core ancestor-traversal diagnosis. It asks
a different question: can an account change file bytes, list a directory, or
remove a known filename? Complete `unlink-notes.md` with predictions and actual
results. The same pauses support independent reading and a paced walkthrough.

## Permission model and equipment

Use an ordinary account in an owned Linux lab with Bash, Python 3.8 or later,
and GNU coreutils. Root is rejected because it can bypass these access checks.
The website IDE edits, saves and exports the files. Preserve `task.sh` beside
`permission_observer.py`; execute them in the external Linux terminal.

For this lab the account owns every generated file and directory. Owner bits
therefore apply. File write permits changing bytes. Directory read permits
listing names; directory search (execute) permits reaching a known child name.
Removing an entry ordinarily requires write and search on its containing
directory, even if the file is read-only. File write alone does not permit
removing its directory entry. This lab uses no sticky directories, ACLs,
read-only mounts, immutable attributes, other accounts or security modules;
those can impose additional rules. Its observations do not establish another
account's access or authorize changes to a service tree.

The program creates only fresh temporary examples under an explicitly supplied
empty owned directory, performs real append/list/unlink operations, records
success or EACCES, and removes its generated examples. It rejects a symlink,
nonempty workspace, unsupported environment or inherited default ACL.

## Predict before running the supplied observation

Predict append, directory listing and unlink for these owner-mode combinations:

| Parent | File | Question |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0700 | 0400 | Can a read-only document's name be removed? |
| 0500 | 0600 | Can bytes change while its name cannot be removed? |
| 0300 | 0400 | Does removing a known name require listing the directory? |

From the extracted role folder, keep the printed workspace path:

~~~bash
lab_root=$(mktemp -d)
printf 'lab_root=%s\n' "$lab_root"
bash task.sh "$lab_root" > access.json 2> access.err
access_status=$?
printf 'status=%s\n' "$access_status"
cat access.err
cat access.json
ls -la -- "$lab_root"
~~~

Verify that the parent is empty again after the run. In the complete result,
observationsCompleted describes actual operations; allPredictionsMatch checks
only the program's model. The starter's named TODO incorrectly predicts unlink
from the file's write bit. Repair it using owner write AND owner search on the
containing directory. Keep the real observations and cleanup unchanged.
Compare the reference only after recording the attempted repair.

Status 0 means the observations completed and the model matched. Status 1 can
still include complete observations when the starter model disagrees. Status 2
means invalid input, an unsupported lab or an incomplete operation; inspect
stderr and do not claim a complete result. Interruption returns 130. None of
these statuses completes the evidence notes automatically.

## Independently observe the actual commands

Create a separate private tree so the program's removed examples are not
mistaken for files available for later inspection:

~~~bash
manual_root=$(mktemp -d)
printf 'manual_root=%s\n' "$manual_root"
mkdir -- "$manual_root/box"
printf 'owned example\n' > "$manual_root/box/document.txt"
chmod 0400 -- "$manual_root/box/document.txt"
chmod 0700 -- "$manual_root/box"
stat -c 'mode=%a uid=%u gid=%g path=%n' -- "$manual_root/box" "$manual_root/box/document.txt"
printf 'probe\n' >> "$manual_root/box/document.txt"
append_status=$?
rm -- "$manual_root/box/document.txt"
unlink_status=$?
printf 'append=%s unlink=%s\n' "$append_status" "$unlink_status"
~~~

The expected append failure is evidence, so use these commands in an ordinary
interactive shell without errexit. Predict and retain each actual status.
Restore the generated document, change just the containing directory and
observe the opposite combination:

~~~bash
printf 'owned example\n' > "$manual_root/box/document.txt"
chmod 0600 -- "$manual_root/box/document.txt"
chmod 0500 -- "$manual_root/box"
printf 'probe\n' >> "$manual_root/box/document.txt"
append_status=$?
rm -- "$manual_root/box/document.txt"
unlink_status=$?
printf 'append=%s unlink=%s\n' "$append_status" "$unlink_status"
cat -- "$manual_root/box/document.txt"
chmod u+w -- "$manual_root/box"
rm -- "$manual_root/box/document.txt"
recovered_status=$?
printf 'recovered unlink=%s\n' "$recovered_status"
~~~

For the third case recreate the file with 0400, set box to 0300, then retain
the actual `ls`, append and `rm` statuses separately. Use the known full
filename. Restore box to 0700 before inspecting or cleaning it. Explain why a
failed listing does not prevent unlink of that known name.

## Changed input, failure and cleanup

Use a second empty path containing a space and compare the same model and
operations. Put a marker file in that workspace, run again and retain the
rejection without deleting the marker. Remove only that owned marker and
repeat to verify recovery:

~~~bash
mkdir -- "$lab_root/with space"
bash task.sh "$lab_root/with space" > changed.json 2> changed.err
printf 'keep\n' > "$lab_root/with space/marker.txt"
bash task.sh "$lab_root/with space" > rejected.json 2> rejected.err
rejected_status=$?
cat -- "$lab_root/with space/marker.txt"
rm -- "$lab_root/with space/marker.txt"
bash task.sh "$lab_root/with space" > recovered.json 2> recovered.err
recovered_status=$?
printf 'rejected=%s recovered=%s\n' "$rejected_status" "$recovered_status"
chmod 0700 -- "$manual_root/box"
printf 'Review before removal: %q\n' "$lab_root" "$manual_root"
rm -r -- "$lab_root" "$manual_root"
~~~

Retain five notes tasks: predictions, the model repair, actual independent
commands, changed/rejected/recovered evidence, and verified cleanup. A supplied
reference method contains no prefilled observations for this run.

Primary reference: [GNU mode structure](https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/html_node/Mode-Structure.html)
and [Linux unlink rules](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/unlink.2.html).

# Creation Masks, Existing Files and Executable Bits

This optional extension follows the permissions core and name-removal
transfer. It investigates initial creation modes rather than ancestor access
or deleting existing entries. Complete `umask-notes.md` with predictions,
actual modes and explanations. The pauses support independent study and a
paced walkthrough.

## What a creation mask changes

Use an ordinary account in an owned Linux lab with Bash, Python 3.8 or later
and GNU stat. Preserve `task.sh` beside `creation_observer.py`. The website IDE
edits, saves and exports these files; run them in the external Linux terminal.

Without a default ACL, a requested mode is filtered by `requested & ~mask`.
This is bit clearing, not decimal or octal subtraction. A regular file created
with requested 0666 does not gain executable bits when mask is 0000. A
directory requested as 0777 can retain search bits. Programs can request other
modes or change them later, so a mask alone does not establish every file's
final mode. Changing a mask does not retroactively change existing files.

The observer creates only fresh temporary examples under an explicit empty
owned workspace. It first creates an existing 0640 document, changes its own
process mask, requests a new 0666 file and 0777 directory, records actual modes
and the existing file's bytes, then restores its inherited mask and removes
its generated tree. It rejects root, symlink/nonempty workspaces and inherited
default ACLs. These observations concern this account and filesystem, not a
service identity or a system-wide policy change.

## Predict and compare actual creation

From the extracted role folder, retain the printed path and caller mask:

~~~bash
lab_root=$(mktemp -d)
printf 'lab_root=%s\n' "$lab_root"
caller_mask=$(umask)
bash task.sh "$lab_root" 0022 > mask-0022.json 2> mask-0022.err
mask_status=$?
printf 'status=%s caller_before=%s caller_after=%s\n' "$mask_status" "$caller_mask" "$(umask)"
cat mask-0022.err
cat mask-0022.json
~~~

Predict 0644 for the new regular file and 0755 for the new directory. Check that the
existing document retains 0640 and its original checksum. The absolute
workspace, inherited mask and observed values must come from this run.

The starter's named TODO incorrectly uses a requested 0777 for a regular
file. Repair that requested mode to match the actual file creation call.
Keep the real mask, actual stat results and restoration unchanged. Compare
the reference after recording a working attempt. Status 0 means completed
observations and a matching model; status 1 can carry a complete result with
a deliberately incorrect starter prediction. Status 2 means invalid input,
an unsupported lab or incomplete operation; inspect stderr. Interruption
returns 130. A matching model does not complete the evidence notes.

## Independently check with Bash and stat

Use a child shell so the experiment does not change the caller's mask:

~~~bash
manual_root=$(mktemp -d)
printf 'manual_root=%s\n' "$manual_root"
printf 'existing data\n' > "$manual_root/existing.txt"
chmod 0640 -- "$manual_root/existing.txt"
(
    umask 0022
    : > "$manual_root/new.txt"
    mkdir -- "$manual_root/new-directory"
~~~

README.md.content:
# Command Lookup, Version Checks and Real Failures

This optional transfer follows the Linux identity and readiness project. It
investigates a tool marked available in a command inventory: which executable
is selected, and does its actual version request succeed? It does not install
software or repeat the shell unit's log-summary project. Complete
`lookup-notes.md` using the prediction, observation and explanation pauses.
The same sequence supports independent reading and a paced walkthrough.

## Equipment and the two observations

Use an ordinary account in an owned Linux lab with Bash and GNU coreutils.
Extract one role with its complete `tools` folder. Read all three tiny supplied
`lab-tool.sh` files before executing them. They are inspected course fixtures,
not downloads or substitutes for installed programs. The website IDE edits,
saves and exports the files; execute the commands in the external Linux lab.

The first tool prints `lab-tool first 1.0`; the second prints
`lab-tool second 2.0`. Both exit 0. The failing tool writes
`controlled version failure` to stderr and exits 23. Each accepts only
`--version`. These controlled outputs isolate lookup from actual execution.
They do not certify that any real course package is installed or trustworthy.

`PATH` is an ordered, colon-separated list of search directories. A slash-free
command name can select a different executable when that order changes. A
shell can also resolve functions, builtins and cached names. This lab uses a
fresh noninteractive Bash for each lookup and run, the fixed external name
`lab-tool.sh`, and only the explicit inspected tool directories. It does not
model every interactive shell's aliases, functions or command cache.

`task.sh` first runs `command -v lab-tool.sh` and retains its status and path.
It then actually runs `lab-tool.sh --version`, retaining the real stdout,
stderr and exit status. A found command can fail. The reference reports usable
only when both observations succeed. Here usable means this version request
succeeded; it does not prove every feature of a program works.

The script changes PATH only in its two child Bash environments. It retains
the absolute path of the running Bash before that change and disables optional
startup-file loading for those children. The calling shell's PATH is unchanged.
It writes no input files, installs nothing and changes no system configuration.

## Predict and observe both search orders

ZIP extraction can omit executable mode bits. From the extracted role folder,
inspect the files, then make only these supplied fixtures executable:

~~~bash
chmod u+x tools/first/lab-tool.sh tools/second/lab-tool.sh tools/failing/lab-tool.sh
role_root=$(pwd -P)
path_before=$PATH
bash task.sh "$role_root/tools/first:$role_root/tools/second" > first.txt 2> first.err
first_status=$?
printf 'report_status=%s\n' "$first_status"
cat first.txt
cat first.err
test "$PATH" = "$path_before"
~~~

Expect lookup status 0, the first tool's path and version, run status 0 and
`usable=yes`. Repeat with second before first, saving different report files.
Predict the changed version before running. Neither order changes the other
tool's contents or any installed program.

## A present command that fails

Put failing before first and save all three channels:

~~~bash
bash task.sh "$role_root/tools/failing:$role_root/tools/first" > failed.txt 2> failed.err
failed_status=$?
printf 'report_status=%s\n' "$failed_status"
cat failed.txt
cat failed.err
~~~

Lookup still succeeds, the failing path is selected, run status is 23, and the
controlled error reaches stderr. The named TODO in the starter checks only
lookup status and incorrectly reports usable with report status 0. Repair that
last condition to require both saved statuses to be 0. Preserve the real tool
calls, their separate statuses and stderr. After repair, expect `usable=no`
and report status 1. Compare the separate reference after saving an attempt.

## Missing command, recovery and transfer

Create a private empty search directory and retain its printed path:

~~~bash
empty_search=$(mktemp -d)
printf 'empty_search=%s\n' "$empty_search"
bash task.sh "$empty_search" > missing.txt 2> missing.err
missing_status=$?
printf 'report_status=%s\n' "$missing_status"
cat missing.txt
cat missing.err
rmdir -- "$empty_search"
~~~

Expect lookup status 1, an empty resolved value, Bash's actual command-not-found
diagnostic and run status 127. The report exits 1. Recover by using the first
tool directory and retain its successful output separately. Do not install a
package to manufacture recovery for this controlled case.

For a changed case, remove execute permission from the first fixture, search
first:second, then restore its original mode. Predict whether the second tool
is selected; record the actual resolved path. Restrict this change to the
inspected course fixture. The script rejects empty, relative, missing, symlink
or unowned directory entries and line breaks; it does not accept a colon as
part of one directory name. Argument errors return 2 before the tool checks.

Complete the five notes tasks with the actual paths, statuses, failure and
recovery. Reopen the saved attempt and verify the original tool bytes and
calling PATH remain intact. Remove only the private case and generated report
files after retaining the evidence. A successful reference run does not fill
in this record or prove the readiness of a real installed tool.

Primary references: [Bash command search](https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/html_node/Command-Search-and-Execution.html),
[Bash command builtin](https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/html_node/Bash-Builtins.html),
and [Bash exit status](https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/html_node/Exit-Status.html).

starter/task.sh.content:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
[[ $(uname -s) == Linux && $EUID -gt 0 ]] || { printf 'Use an ordinary account in an owned Linux lab.\n' >&2; exit 2; }
if (( $# != 1 )); then
    printf 'usage: bash task.sh ABSOLUTE_SEARCH_DIRECTORY[:DIRECTORY...]\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
search_path=$1
[[ -n $search_path && $search_path != :* && $search_path != *: && $search_path != *::* && $search_path != *$'\n'* && $search_path != *$'\r'* ]] || { printf 'Use nonempty absolute directory entries without line breaks.\n' >&2; exit 2; }
IFS=: read -r -a search_directories <<< "$search_path"
for directory in "${search_directories[@]}"; do
    [[ $directory == /* && -d $directory && ! -L $directory && -O $directory ]] || { printf 'Use owned ordinary absolute search directories.\n' >&2; exit 2; }
done
readonly bash_bin=$BASH
if resolved=$(PATH="$search_path" BASH_ENV=/dev/null "$bash_bin" --noprofile --norc -c 'command -v lab-tool.sh'); then
    lookup_status=0
else
    lookup_status=$?
fi
printf 'lookup_status=%s\nresolved=%s\n' "$lookup_status" "$resolved"
if PATH="$search_path" BASH_ENV=/dev/null "$bash_bin" --noprofile --norc -c 'lab-tool.sh --version'; then
    run_status=0
else
    run_status=$?
fi
printf 'run_status=%s\n' "$run_status"
# TODO: a located command can still fail its actual version request.
if (( lookup_status == 0 )); then
    printf 'usable=yes\n'
    exit 0
fi
printf 'usable=no\n'
exit 1
